summary:
Imo State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies in full and reaches well beyond marriage. Human Rights Watch records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and documents police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under it. The UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment. Sharia criminal law, under which male sodomy carries the death penalty in twelve northern states, does not extend to Imo, a southern state.

Enforcement in Imo is recent and active. On 19 February 2025 the Imo Police Command reported foiling a same-sex party at Graziella Hotels, Orogwe, in Owerri West, arresting what it described as many gay and lesbian suspects and placing attendees who fled on a police search list. The command gave no precise figure for those arrested, and no court outcome from that raid has been sourced.

Community vigilantism runs alongside state action. In April 2018 two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets accused of gay sex; a NoStringsNG inquiry found that the victims were themselves arrested by police and might need legal support. A crowd assault therefore ended in police processing of the men who had been attacked.

Dating applications are an identified entrapment channel nationwide. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Official foreign guidance reflects the exposure: the UK FCDO travel advice warns of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states (Sahara Reporters, August 2026).

Presentation alone can draw police attention. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility. Reuters (September 2022) records that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing, which would make appearance itself a discrete offence. Those proposals are not sourced as enacted law.

Lethal violence against a visibly transgender woman has gone unpunished. The beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in August 2024 hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough investigation. In February 2025 The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement across Nigeria takes the form of mass arrests at social venues, a pattern Imo sits inside. Wikipedia's country coverage records more than 100 party-goers arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that dissolved by the end of 2011.

A decade-outcome assessment of the statute exists. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024) finds that the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.

Venues and organisations that serve LGBTQ+ people face closure by exposure. The House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008; some members were threatened, beaten and stoned.

Placement of a transgender prisoner raised questions an official panel took up. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison in Lagos and was released on 5 August 2024. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
localsOnly:
The SSMPA's ban on operating gay organisations constrains resident organising directly, and activists say the Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and their allies to abandon community health and education work.

Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes to police, which removes the ordinary protection pathways that residents otherwise rely on.

Employment exposure is documented: LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects in the decade since the 2014 statute, alongside increased attacks.

Residents who are publicly identified face sustained risk. Members of the House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church had their names and addresses printed in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and were subsequently threatened, beaten and stoned, prompting the church to cancel conferences.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory establishes an SSMPA conviction or sentence arising in Imo State; the February 2025 Orogwe raid has no sourced court outcome, and the number of people arrested in it is unresolved beyond the police command's own wording.

The legal support needs identified after the April 2018 Imo street assault are unresolved: whether the two men were prosecuted, released or assisted is not sourced.

The cross-dressing proposals reported in September 2022 are not sourced as enacted legislation, in Imo or nationally; their current legislative status is unresolved.

Imo-specific provisions on gender markers, identity documents, name change, bathroom access or medical care for visitors are not sourced in this inventory and remain unresolved.

Whether the 'kito' app entrapment pattern reported in April 2024 has been documented specifically within Imo State is not sourced.
